Industry News: Endurance Athletes and the Myth of the Invincible Heart

📅 24 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 20 min read (4078 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Outsideonline

⏱️ ~20 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • (Photo: 3dMediSphere/Science Photo Library / Getty).
  • It has been revealed that seth Ruhling was ten days away from racing in the 2023 World Mountain Running Championships when he first felt the pain.
  • Sources indicate that the next morning, Ruhling pulled on his scrubs and went to work.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

(Photo: 3dMediSphere/Science Photo Library / Getty).

It has been revealed that seth Ruhling was ten days away from racing in the 2023 World Mountain Running Championships when he first felt the pain. It woke him up. It tingled down his arm. It ached along the whole length of his spine. A nurse working out of the operating room at a local hospital in Louisville, Colorado, Ruhling took an aspirin just to be safe. Surely, he thought, this is not a heart thing. He got up and rolled out his back. He didn’t think much of it. He went to sleep.

Sources indicate that the next morning, Ruhling pulled on his scrubs and went to work. The pain had not relented. He turned to one of the doctors on his floor and described the symptoms. The pain in his chest, the way it hurt when he bent over. At best, the doctor stated, it’s nothing. At worst, he continued, you’re having an aortic dissection and you are about to die. Ruhling walked across the building and checked himself into his own hospital’s emergency room.

The answer was somewhere in between. Electrocardiograms (EKGs) and blood work told the story of a potential heart attack. Nurses and doctors who Ruhling knew personally turned, in that moment, from coworkers to aides. They hovered over him, checking in. It was then that Ruhling thought, maybe the worst is happening. He started mentally preparing himself. He realized he should call his wife in case he died. Thankfully, the worst was not happening. Despite the fact that so many of the signs pointed to a heart attack, those same signs also pointed to Ruhling’s official diagnosis: pericarditis—an inflammation of the pericardium, a sac of fibrous tissue that surrounds and protects the heart.

Industry observers note that in essence, the heart is a simple enough thing. A muscle that can be made stronger so that you can live longer. This is why it is the subject of metaphor, of symbolism. The heart as the soul; the heart as the ticking second clock of our lives. The heart as what you care about the most, and the heart as what makes you capable of care at all. But in reality, the heart is a many-layered thing of rooms. There are parts of the heart that sound as if they are craters on the Moon. Superior Vena Cava. Fossa Ovalis. Vena Cordis Magna. Sometimes, in the darkness, listening to the sound of my own heartbeat, I cannot stand the mystery. I turn on a fan to cut out the noise. It is strange that something is ticking inside of me without my permission. It is stranger still that I depend on it. Even stranger still that, if it stopped, so would I.

For runners and endurance sport athletes, the heart is one of the most measured things on the planet. It starts with heart rate but continues with heart rate variability, cardiac output, stroke volume, and more. I imagine most serious runners could tell you their resting heart rate and their max heart rate, that they could look at you mid-run, without glancing at their watch, and tell you where exactly their heart rate is pinned, entirely by feel alone. One-hundred-forty beats per minute. One-hundred-fifty-two. One-hundred-sixty-five, their chest heaving as they say the words. And yet, for all this data, I also imagine that most endurance athletes take their heart for granted. They worry about sore tendons and ligaments, the stress a bone might be bearing, and whether or not their piriformis will continue to remain as tight as it feels. An injured heart is out of the question. It awaits us later in life, maybe. Surely not now. But what happens when it’s the heart that’s the matter? The heart—the very soul of it all?

Sources indicate that years ago, attending the funeral of my wife’s grandfather, I blacked out and came to with a paramedic standing over me. I was splayed and sweating in the middle of a church, and there he was, his face in my face, a man I had never seen before. His hat—I will never forget—was the kind of Red Sox hat only true loyalists can ever hope to wear, a hat so worn and sun-stained that it contained every shade of red and every shade of blue. The funeral went on as I was attended to. People filed into the aisle for communion as I was shepherded into a back room and then into an ambulance. Before he wheeled me into the emergency room, the paramedic slapped me on the shoulder. “Good luck, buddy,” he mentioned, “you’re probably going to need a pacemaker for the rest of your life.” I looked up at his face against the cool blue of the sky and felt a fear I could not understand. I had run, up to that point, 21 marathons, over a dozen ultras, more than 100 miles in a day. Surely, I thought, this can’t be my heart.

In a recent development, for over a day, I stayed in a hospital and moved from one room to another as people studied my heart. Somewhere many floors below the ground, a man rubbed gel over my chest and used an instrument that turned the inside of my body into a beating, pulsing thing on a screen. I couldn’t look at it; I felt naked and dreadfully exposed. I spent the night in a room next to an older man whose heart was failing him and whose response to such failure was an anger that bordered on rage. People were worried; I was distraught. Later, I ran on a treadmill as it ascended to an impossible gradient. I was wearing hospital underwear that kept falling off and dozens of wires that dripped with sweat. Everything beeped. I was very stressed; it was called a stress test. For weeks, I walked around with a lump under intentionally baggy clothes: a monitor; it measured every beep, even while I slept.

Some say that each person is born with a predetermined number of heartbeats. That the heart is perpetually counting down. That one day, at a given number, it will stop. If this is true, then runners and cyclists and people out there expending effort over miles and miles and miles are people who play with fire—going out each day into the world to increase their heart rate in the hope that, for every waking and sleeping hour that follows, their heart rate will be lower for all of that raising. The heart is simple enough when it works in this way, beating faster and then slower, working for you as you work and then resting with you as you rest. This is the way it is supposed to go—in the background, without your consideration or your knowledge. But really, the heart is a terrifying thing. Because of this fact, you learn, I think, to forget it, the way you forget about your breath. But when you cannot forget it? When you are made to be reminded? You think about how fine the line is upon which you walk. The truth is that we all live there, on that slim thread, our broken bodies ticking like broken clocks.

According to recent reports, it is perhaps an all-too-common assumption to think that runners and cyclists are immune from injuries of the heart, that their sport protects the heart, strengthening it rather than hurting it. But lately, the hearts of such athletes have been thrust into the limelight. Jenny Simpson, one of the most lauded middle-distance runners in American history, collapsed earlier this year while running at the Sir Walter Running Pop-Up Mile. She had gone into cardiac arrest and would later go into cardiac arrest again while at the hospital. Her diagnosis: arrhythmogenic right ventricular cardiomyopathy—a life-threatening condition brought on by scar tissue in the heart. She will never race, let alone run, again. A few months later, while racing UTMB, one of the most prestigious and grueling ultramarathons in the world, Jeff Browning, a fixture at the top of the ultrarunning circuit for years on end, suffered a heart attack. Surgery and multiple hospital stays soon followed. He may run again, but it will not be the same.

It is that sameness you lose when you are reminded that you have a heart, and that it can be broken. There is a before, and there is an after. In that blissful before-time, your heart is your superpower. You can run for hours—so why wouldn’t you have a heart so strong that it doesn’t need to be considered? So strong that you can assume it is one of the best things working within you? It takes one moment, one diagnosis, one brief bit of faltering to leave such a moment of naivety and enter whatever comes after. It takes fainting in a church, back pain just days before you are supposed to race up a mountain. Wearing that heart rate monitor after my hospital stay, I walked around with a kind of shame, covering my body up with sweaters, not wanting myself—or anyone—to know that this ticking, beating muscle I had once taken for granted might be broken. I listened carefully to it, like I never had before. I hardly slept. I felt everything that could be a murmur, some aberration. Everything changes when it is your heart that’s the matter.

There’s no way that can be my heart. That’s what Megan Roche thought when, not long after one of the best 20-mile training runs of her life, her chest ached suddenly and sharply. She denied the possibility for days, refusing to go to the hospital, until she was forced to walk up hills she used to run over. It was then that she went to an emergency room and was diagnosed with myocarditis—inflammation of the heart muscle itself, rather than the lining of the muscle. She took six months off of running. She had a baby. She rested. She felt better. She was ready to return to her competitive form. But then, over the next five years, she suffered six different bouts of recurrent pericarditis, including the most recent one, earlier this year, which landed her in the hospital with a cardiac catheter.

Sources indicate that she is back on the mend, racing and running again, but not without the existential meditation that such an injury brings on. For Roche, her injured heart has called into question her running mortality—the thin fragility of one of the very things that gives her life meaning. “I think it’s made me contemplate: What would it look like to exist in a life without running?” she remarked. “A lot of people have been there for various reasons, and this one just feels so visceral. At the end of the day, I’d be OK with it. I don’t think I’m going to die from pericarditis, but I do think it could end my athletic career. I’ve processed that running mortality so many different times.”.

In a recent development, dr. Jason Tso, the Medical Director of Stanford’s Sports Cardiology program, has seen plenty of endurance athletes who are processing that same feeling. He studies the relationship between extended endurance exercise and the heart. The science, he told me, is still developing, but it has become clear that all endurance sports carry some degree of cardiac risk. Tso rattled off a bunch of conditions that endurance athletes see more of than regular folks: AFib, coronary disease, calcified coronary disease. All of these are more common in endurance athletes, and specifically male athletes. I had a hard time listening to him, thinking of all the miles I had logged and all the ways that I thought they made me better, fitter, healthier. It felt like some strange, uncanny world, where what you thought was good for you was actually bad—everything upside down, the heart hating the person that tried to make it stronger. “There are really only a few things that exercise probably makes worse,” said Tso. “And pericarditis and myocarditis—heart inflammation—that’s one of them.”.

“But if you also look at it, healthy athletes live longer than non-athletes,” continued Tso. He supposed the following: that, maybe, despite the fact that athletes are diagnosed with certain heart ailments more frequently than non-athletes, they’re not, as he mentioned, “dropping dead all the time from them.” Maybe, Tso wondered, their fitness and health offer some protection against the magnitude of certain diseases. One recent study, in the European Heart Journal, backs up this claim. In two groups of people with pericarditis, those who were athletes had fewer instances of recurrence than those who were not.

And yet, even if exercise doesn’t make your heart issue worse, it seems that mentally, there’s no real way to forget a heart incident. “I remember going on runs a couple months later, and every once in a while, you just have a thought pop in your head: What if this is worse than they said?” Ruhling told me. “When it’s your heart, there’s so much more unknown.”.

It took him a long time to get to a place where he didn’t think of his heart, which also meant that he didn’t think of dying.

Recent findings suggest that dying is the scary word here. It took me just over 2,000 words to write that one word, but dying is the word that kept me up at night those years ago, my monitor fixed to my chest, measuring every beat. I was thinking about dying. It’s a word that is inseparable from the heart, mostly—and paradoxically—because the heart is inseparable from life. My wife and I welcomed a baby boy into our lives earlier this year, and it was his heart we heard first—this pulsing, undulating, flickering little thing on a screen, beating away at 160 times a minute when it was not much larger than a sesame seed. “He’s working hard,” the doctor remarked. “He’s growing.” Now, putting him down to sleep, I place my hand atop his chest and listen for it, still hammering away, this reckless and beautiful sign of life that indicates I am here and I am working hard and I am growing.

At some point, I think, we stop putting our hands on our own chests. We take our hearts for granted, which means we take our lives, too, for granted. One breath becomes another until we are 30, 40, 50 years old, unaware that we are waiting for the day to be reminded that there are a finite number of days in our finite lives. This reminder is akin to Megan Roche’s idea of “running mortality”—this notion that we practice letting go all of the time. We practice being finite, fragile, and futile. Even the things that bring us joy might come with a second-hand ticking away alongside them. The heart has that second-hand built into its architecture. It is a reminder that the word “mortality” sits next to everything we do.

Mike Foote—who finished third at UTMB in 2012 and has placed second at the prestigious Hardrock 100 three times—is still contemplating his own running mortality. In 2024, after a multi-day fastpacking trip out in the mountains, Foote started to feel chest pain that then radiated down his back. His workups came back with the same diagnosis as Ruhling—pericarditis—and he was told not to allow his heart rate past 110 beats per minute for months. For an endurance athlete, this feels like some kind of unholy punishment. A brisk walk can push the heart rate above 100 or 110. “It took the wind out of my sails,” Foote told me. “It was really stubborn and smoldering and not really wanting to go away.”.

According to recent reports, even after the months of recovery, his pericarditis kept coming back. At a specialty clinic, Foote was told that the goal for pericarditis patients was for them to be able to walk around at the mall, not to run up a mountain. It echoed something Roche told me—that, during her bout of myocarditis, even walking up the small hill of her driveway was one of the hardest things on earth.

Recent findings suggest that “It’s hard,” Foote told me, “having to decouple from that identity and the loss of opportunities to be social with friends. There’s just a whole other component to it that was also really hard to navigate. I mean, anybody with an injury can identify with that, but this one was so long and so uncertain. I was like—oh, I just might never run again.”.

In a recent development, for Foote, pericarditis might forever change his relationship not just to running, but also to his life. “I’ve had echocardiograms done and all these other things that show that I have a really strong, efficient heart,” he said. And yet, because of his relative inactivity, so many of those once-strong numbers associated with his heart health have regressed. “That’s really scary,” he said. “Not only do I feel these symptoms, but here’s objective data of my heart becoming less healthy in just the last year.”.

It has been revealed that it’s difficult for him not to be anxious about it. Though he still worries about returning to running now, he worries more about his health, his lifestyle, and his ability to be active with those he loves. “What does this mean about how I am with my family?” Foote noted. “What does this mean for my lifespan?”.

Not long after racing in the Unbound Gravel Race in Emporia, Kansas, Keith Kelly—former NCAA Division 1 Cross Country champion at Providence College—was out on an easy bike ride. He had left the sport of running a long time before, beleaguered by constant injuries, the kinds of things runners might expect but don’t hope for: cartilage damage, knee pain, joints worn until they’re just bone on bone. He had faced enough injury in his life, and the switch to biking gave him great joy, and a pain-free future of sport that he could imagine. On that ride, though, Kelly started not to feel like himself, his body working harder than it should’ve, a strange sensation in his chest. He looked at his Garmin bike computer to find that his heart rate was pegged at a whopping 234 beats a minute. The last time he checked, he was not a hummingbird.

It kept happening. He’d stand up from the couch, and his chest would vibrate in this unsettling way. Drink a beer, chest humming and hopping. Zone one ride on Zwift, barely trying to break a sweat—chest rattling in its cage. Keith Kelly had AFib. His heart, for minutes on end, would short-circuit, zipping and zapping and misfiring all over the place. When it happened, Kelly would ask his wife to place her hand on his chest, and she could feel it, too. He was anxious. She was anxious. Kelly felt no small amount of doom. How surreal it was to be going about your day, relaxing on the couch, only to stand and find yourself in the middle of an episode where the inside of your body—that ticking, perfect clock of the soul—could not get the ticking right. Kelly remembered his countless knee surgeries, how his joint had little to no cartilage. He had been forced to hang up his spikes, to give up running and racing for good. But this was different. When the injury was his heart, it felt like it could strike senselessly, in the midst of a blue sky day, and become all he could think about. It felt, too, like the worst could happen. He didn’t even want to think about it. It was his heart, after all.

After months of doctor’s visits and heart-rate monitoring and waiting, Kelly had an ablation. Doctors threaded a little zapper, as he called it, through his groin and up an artery, where they shocked the parts of his heart that were misfiring. It worked. He woke up, he said, as if from a nap. He’s back riding now. He’s holding out hope.

In the end, perhaps the real truth is that no joy comes without some degree of risk. It’s hard to comprehend the fact that risks lives everywhere, even in the midst of activities that seem to be geared toward mitigating such risk. Sudden cardiac deaths during marathons are not common at all—one study found 176 incidents of cardiac arrest, which were not always fatal, among over 29 million marathon runners—and yet, when such incidents happen, they garner significant media attention. They make even the most seemingly healthy activity feel like it hovers close to the edge of mortality. And even as endurance sports mitigate some health risks, the increased volume of exercise may influence the possibility of hurting not just your ligaments and tendons and bones, but also your heart. One study linking excessive endurance training to AFib risk names this a “paradoxical phenomenon”—that the more someone engages in “high-volume endurance training,” the more likely they are to contract AFib. Another study offers the picture of a “U-shaped relationship.” Too much endurance activity, and you’re at risk of AFib. Too little endurance activity—also at risk of AFib.

I guess every activity in this world should come with some sort of warning label that asks: What risk are you willing to take on? For runners and endurance athletes alike, is it the increased risk of an unhealthy heart by not running marathons? Or the ever-present possibility of some kind of heart injury because of running and training for marathons? In a culture so fixated on biohacking and maxxing, fitness can seem like some endless pursuit of invincibility, where every metric can be fine-tuned and optimized in the hope that nothing bad will happen at all. And yet, even then, as Dr. Tso told me with a kind of wryness: “Some of these guys go keto, and their cholesterol numbers look…I don’t even know how they get that bad—it’s horrible.” Even if the body can go the distance, can lose the weight, can digest the food—the heart might pay the price.

All of these athletes share a kind of suddenness, a sharp demarcation between the moment their heart was their superpower and their heart was the matter, when the heart moved from being the unthinking engine behind all their miles into something inflamed or broken or twitching or scarred. Sports remind us that we live in frail and fragile bodies as often as they remind us that we live in strong and valiant ones, but they don’t often remind us that we live, always, in mortal ones. For the ones who have recovered, like Seth Ruhling and Keith Kelly, they move forward with burn marks on their heart, traumatic memories of thinking about one’s final words to one’s wife. And then there are the ones whose recovery is ongoing, who place words like “mortality” next to words like “running” and wonder if any of it—life or sport—will ever be the same again. This is the power, I think, of beautiful things. Beating things inside of us with names that belong on the moon. Their influence swings in two directions; they are paradoxical phenomena; they give us life, and, with a sharpness, remind us that those same lives can end.

Industry observers note that I get a heart workup every year now as a part of my annual physical. It scares the shit out of me. I tell myself to be brave, but I ready myself for the worst. I expect to hear of inflamed things, vibrating things, enlarged things—these injuries to the heart, an organ invisible to us as it keeps us alive. Everything has been good lately, but I get worried for when it won’t be, which, I guess, is true of everything. Maybe that’s part of what makes the heart so apt for metaphor and symbolism. It keeps you alive, and yet it is easy to forget about. But when it fails, briefly, or when it trembles or murmurs or swells or aches—it becomes the only thing you think about. We take it for granted—how much goes into this whole thing we call being alive. Taking for granted is a kind of forgetting. For people who know the pain of the heart, there is no forgetting. There is only living, which is another word for the space between two heartbeats.

#182217. Zion Draws The Crowds—These 3 Nearby Parks Are Where to Escape Them

📅 23 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 5m • 📚 Deep Dive (1084 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Backpacker ↗ Open Full Page

Zion Draws The Crowds—These 3 Nearby Parks Are Where to Escape Them

📅 23 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (1084 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Backpacker

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • According to recent reports, just beyond Zion lie some truly incredible desert landscapes to wander without the crowds.
  • Entry queues and crowded trails come with the territory at bucket-list national parks like Zion.
  • Sources indicate that but I’ll be honest: On my recent trip to Zion, the trails felt more like a conga line than a wilderness escape.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, just beyond Zion lie some truly incredible desert landscapes to wander without the crowds. (Photo: Arrterra via Getty).

Entry queues and crowded trails come with the territory at bucket-list national parks like Zion. With nearly 5 million visitors in 2025, it ranked as the second-most visited national park in the U.S. Once you make it through the entry gate, though, the payoff is real. Visitors walk beneath towering Navajo sandstone cliffs and wade the Virgin River deep into The Narrows. If luck’s on your side, you might even win the permit lottery to hike to Angels Landing.

Sources indicate that but I’ll be honest: On my recent trip to Zion, the trails felt more like a conga line than a wilderness escape. I was more paranoid than peaceful, constantly stepping aside and watching my footing as I squeezed past other hikers. The incredible beauty of the park draws equally incredible crowds.

Industry observers note that the good news is you don’t have to fight for elbow room to soak in Zion’s beauty. Its neighboring state parks, wildernesses, and national forests get a fraction of the attention, but are just as jaw-dropping. Explore the surrounding Greater Zion region, and you’ll unlock hikes through red rock without the gridlock.

Head beyond Zion for these underrated hiking spots instead.

Distance from Zion: 1 hour (West) Entrance fee: $15 per vehicle Best for: Hikers seeking desert variety without a grueling trek. Petrified dunes, sandstone cliffs, slot canyons, and hikeable lava tubes, all in one park.

It has been revealed that if Snow Canyon State Park were a DJ, it’d spin a killer geological mashup of 180-million-year-old petrified dunes, Jurassic-period sandstone escarpments, and ancient river-carved slot canyons. The drop: cavernous, jet-black lava tubes you can hike into (headlamp recommended). The park packs a huge punch of diverse terrain you rarely see all in one place. It’s especially family-friendly and a good fit for more casual hikers who want photo-worthy views without a grueling trek.

Recent findings suggest that catch the park’s greatest hits in one go by linking up the Butterfly Trail, Lava Flow Overlook, West Canyon Overlook, and the Petrified Dunes Loop. The roughly 3-mile loop connects the park’s most notable features. Hikers will see ancient lava flows, winding slickrock passages, and sweeping views down into West Canyon. The petrified dunes along the route steal the show. Hikers walk over rolling hills frozen in time while swirling stripes of orange, cream, and crimson dance underfoot.

Industry observers note that looking for more technical hiking? Tackle the trek to Deidre Peak. The 7.4-mile out-and-back climbs nearly 1,500 feet in elevation and requires a Class 3-4 scramble over rugged sandstone outcrops. The trail crosses into the larger Red Cliffs Desert Reserve, a conservation area protected as a sanctuary for the native Mojave desert tortoise.

Distance from Zion: 1 hour (West) Entrance fee: $5 per vehicle Best for: Hikers and BLM land lovers seeking seclusion and solitude.

Beyond Snow Canyon sprawls Red Cliffs National Conservation Area. The nearly 45,000 acres of BLM land sits within the larger Red Cliffs Desert Reserve at the crossroads of the Mojave Desert, Great Basin, and Colorado Plateau. Here you’ll find a mix of plants and wildlife from all three regions. There are two endangered wildflowers that grow only in this corner of Utah: the dwarf bear poppy and Shivwits milkvetch. Both bloom in spring, with peak overlap in late April and early May. Then there’s southern Utah’s classic red sandstone stretching as far as the eye can see.

Popular out-and-back hikes like the 3.5-mile Elephant Arch Trail and 1.6-mile Red Reef Trail show how water and wind erosion turn sandstone landscapes into works of art. Elephant Arch earned its name from a distinct sandstone outcropping that looks uncannily like a trunk, head, and ears. Along the Red Reef Trail, hikers skirt massive, smooth sandstone bowls. These turn into swimming holes during spring rain and monsoon season, which runds July through September.

Industry observers note that the 5-mile Black Gulch and Yellow Knolls Loop drops through a boulder-strewn gulch of dark volcanic rock, then rolls over yellow sandstone knolls. Hikers can also link the Red Reef and Prospector Trails to create a 10.5-mile loop requiring some scrambling and route-finding through remote backcountry canyons. On the return leg, wide views open up to the Pine Valley Mountains in the north, often capped with snow in winter and early spring.

Distance from Zion: 1 hour 15 minutes (Northeast) Entrance fee: None Best for: Hikers looking for trail variety that showcases Utah’s finest terrain.

Industry observers note that the state’s largest national forest shows off a completely different side of southern Utah. Dixie National Forest sprawls across nearly 2 million acres, rising from the desert valley around St. George to peaks above 11,000 feet. Sagebrush, pinyon, and juniper give way to aspen groves and conifer forests as you climb. The higher and farther you hike, the more surprises you’ll find: trout-filled mountain lakes, towering hoodoo spires, and the chance to spot Utah prairie dogs in the wild.

Dixie gives hikers a taste of the same pink-and-orange Claron limestone that made Bryce Canyon famous. The difference? Here, thick stands of ponderosa pine grow right up against the hoodoos. Plus, the trails see a fraction of the foot traffic, so you’ll have the views practically to yourself.

If you want more hoodoo action, check out Thunder Mountain Trail. It winds through what feels like a bite-sized Bryce Canyon. The out-and-back trail climbs more than 1,700 feet over 8.6 miles. You’re rewarded with an unforgettable trek through a maze of spires. For an even more awe-inspiring experience, hike early or late in the day, when low sun turns the Claron limestone a vibrant orange.

Looking for a more Zion-esque experience? Ashdown Gorge Trail echoes the Narrows, minus the permits, rental gear, and crowds. It travels 10 miles from the alpine rim of Cedar Breaks to a creek-carved canyon where red rock walls close in overhead. Heads up: There are two popular ways to hike Ashdown Gorge. You can do an out-and-back that starts at the bottom and heads up into the narrows (recommended), or a point-to-point that requires a shuttle.

For a longer, relatively flat dayhike, opt for the 11-mile Navajo Lake Loop. The trail circles its namesake, peeking in and out of dense pine, fir, and aspen forest, with shoreline views that make it easy to forget you’re in a red rock wonderland.

#182216. Industry News: The Best Affordable Ski Trips Across the U.S.

📅 24 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 8m • 📚 Deep Dive (1529 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Outsideonline ↗ Open Full Page

Industry News: The Best Affordable Ski Trips Across the U.S.

📅 24 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 8 min read (1529 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Outsideonline

⏱️ ~8 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Skiers and boarders are gushing about El Niño again.
  • While early signs do suggest that an epic season might be coming, we won’t know for sure until frequent storms continue to dump snow.
  • In a recent development, climate change is shifting weather patterns, making snow forecasts more challenging.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Bogus Basin at sunset (Photo: Steve Bly / Getty).

Skiers and boarders are gushing about El Niño again. The 2026-2027 winter won’t involve just any ENSO but a so-called Super El Niño. Potentially the biggest one on record, with exceptionally warm ocean temps on the West Coast hopefully sending a turbocharged jet stream across the U.S. According to my skiing friends, bartenders, and Trader Joe’s clerks, this could become the most memorable El Niño of our lives. Maybe.

While early signs do suggest that an epic season might be coming, we won’t know for sure until frequent storms continue to dump snow. It’s also uncertain where these potential storms may fall, though an El Niño typically sends winter weather toward the southern half of the country. Another question is whether a chance at great conditions warrants the risk of pricey reservations. And let’s be honest, we’ve all been burned before. Especially in recent years.

In a recent development, climate change is shifting weather patterns, making snow forecasts more challenging. Rising global temps are causing more rain to fall at higher elevations. Meanwhile, skiing mega-corps have acquired most substantial-name resorts around the country, driving up lift tickets and inviting allegations of price-fixing. Plus, mountain town gentrification and nationwide inflation have skyrocketed the cost of lodging and meals out.

Industry observers note that the estimated expense of an annual weeklong ski trip for a family of four now ranges from around $5,000 to over $15,000! That’s roughly the same budget as a small destination wedding, if you married a new person every single year. No surprise, last season’s poor Western conditions saw many Americans separating from the ski industry, with winter resort visits reportedly falling 9.1 percent below the ten-year average.

It has been revealed that despite the rising rates, there are still ways to initiative an affordable ski trip. As a member of a self-certified band of dirtbag skiers (along with my friends, bartenders, and Trader Joe’s clerks), I’ve spent years chasing powder on the cheap. During winter road trips around the country, I’ve slept inside my pickup cap, searched for seedy motels, earned backcountry turns, and skied lesser-known resorts. Here are a few ideas for budget-friendly ski trips, plus some tips for finding more options on your own.

Sources indicate that colorado is considered the main character in U.S. skiing, typically accruing the most resort visits each year. Many of the best-known ski mountains are here, including Breck, Keystone, Steamboat, etc. The state is home to the two mega-pass conglomerates, the Epic Pass controlled by Vail and the Ikon Pass controlled by Alterra. Full passes cost over $1,000, plus staying in premier destinations often involves eye-popping price tags.

For years, friends and I explored the state with the reasonable but sadly discontinued Rocky Mountain Super Pass Plus. Other seasons, I ventured across the West using the early Mountain Collective Pass (today’s version is pricier but still includes top resorts). We mostly skied the significant famous mountains while learning to stay down the road in cheaper towns. After the corporate-acquisitions era of recent decades, it seemed like affordable skiing road trips might be a thing of the past.

Industry observers note that then came the Indy Pass in 2019-2020, which has become an impressive and economical multi-pass focused on independent and smaller resorts. The concept is not just staying further out but skiing down the road, too. New customers must join a waitlist. In the meantime, glancing at the Indy resort map can lead you to many budget destinations.

It has been revealed that down the road from Aspen, near Glenwood Springs, consider Sunlight Mountain. The smaller acreage means smaller prices, crowds, and stats—yet it still has steeps. Being lower in elevation, you’ll want to watch the weather to catch the best conditions, a sound practice in general.

Industry observers note that further west, at the edge of the Rockies, try skiing off the Grand Mesa at Powderhorn. Instead of Crested Butte, go up the road to the ridiculously high-elevation Monarch Mountain, helpful if the storms are running warm. And far to the south, away from all significant resorts, check out Wolf Creek, known for capturing the most snow in Colorado.

Recent findings suggest that another way to find bargain skiing is to bypass the famous Rockies or Sierra and aim for lesser-known mountain ranges. This approach was thrust upon me when I left NorCal, where I grew up, and moved to the Midwest for grad school. Later, my wife and I relocated to the Southeast for her professor job.

According to recent reports, when it comes to the East, what has been called the “Ice Coast” now supplements or exceeds its natural totals with advanced snow-making equipment. A good example is Western North Carolina. Outside Boone, the fun Beech Mountain is the East’s highest ski resort, with a microbrewery resting atop its 5,506-foot summit. Their weekday 4-hour flex pass is among the best deals in the Southern Appalachians. Meanwhile, toward the northern side of that range, Vermont has several budget options, including Burke Mountain, Jay Peak, and Smugglers’ Notch.

My favorite area in the East is at the moment the Alleghenies in West Virginia. Now owned by Alterra, Snowshoe has the biggest name, terrain, and associated expenses. About two hours north, an affordable alternative is a trio of resorts around Canaan Valley. Modernized Timberline Mountain has fast lifts, solid terrain, and ski-in lodgings that attract weekend D.C. crowds. Midweek is quieter and includes gift-card rebates.

Sources indicate that the valley’s unique outlier is White Grass, an inexpensive ski touring area with 1,200 feet of vert, a mix of groomed and natural trails, and several peaks to skin up and ski off. The middle-ground gem is old-school Canaan Valley Ski Resort, a state park property with a reasonable lodge on-site plus all the best-of-budget features: slow creaky lifts, moderate stats, and mandatory traverses to reach the widespread and tree-lined trails.

While living cash-strapped in St. Louis, Missouri, I learned to be extra-creative about winter sports. Outside the city, I skied with upcoming pals at tiny Hidden Valley. (“Still looking for it,” we’d joke, but we were happy to have anything.) Graciously, the locals shared some surprising options around the Midwest. Chestnut Mountain overlooking the Mississippi River in Galena, Illinois. Sporty Granite Peak in Wisconsin. The lake-effect Mount Bohemia on Michigan’s Upper Peninsula, where a window ticket costs about the same as an early-bird season pass—approximately $100!

Ditching the “biggest-mountains-or-nothing” mindset can lead you to other deals around the country. In recent years, my investigation into the mysterious cross-continental journey of Native explorer Moncacht-Apé led me repeatedly to Idaho. Simultaneously, I was scouting for future skiing around the unsung Snake River Plain, which may fall on the edge of this season’s El Niño storm tracks.

According to recent reports, located on a ridge north of Boise, Bogus Basin is a nonprofit ski area with vast acreage, fast lifts, and solid terrain. That said, its lower base elevation, around 6,000 feet, mandates condition peeping. About 16 miles downhill, the booming city of Boise is primarily a summer destination, meaning there’s usually a glut of affordable lodgings during winter.

Staying in such warm-weather hotspots, including college sports towns, is another way to consistently pull off cheaper ski trips. With this approach, glancing around the Snake River Plain reveals several more budget options. South of Twin Falls, there are two smaller areas: Magic Mountain and Pomerelle. Rising above Pocatello, aka the friendly college town called “Pokey,” you’ll find the challenging wildcard of Pebble Creek.

It has been revealed that once you start searching for winter deals, you’ll discover some pretty fun choices. Along the winding Mt. Rose Highway, there’s a pair of hidden resorts within striking distance of the “Biggest Little City in the World.” Just 30 minutes from downtown Reno, the closest option is Mt. Rose, a local favorite with Tahoe’s highest base at 8,260 feet. The scenery is top-notch, and the higher elevation often leads to better snow.

Everything else is middle-of-the-pack, and, as we’ve seen, aiming for this level is a reliable way to find affordable skiing. The crowds at Mt. Rose are smaller, particularly midweek. The terrain and stats are solid. The pricing is manageable, especially for Tahoe and when factoring in daily specials like two-for-one Tuesday or Ladies Thursday.

In a recent development, the situation is similar at the smaller Diamond Peak, about 15 minutes further downhill near Incline Village. The lakeside views are expansive, though the prices aren’t quite as good and the lower 6,700-foot base means you should monitor temps and conditions.

It has been revealed that for the cost of driving, you can skip expensive Tahoe lodging and usually find ridiculously low winter rates around Reno. I once snagged a high-rise casino room for $30 per night. After the slopes, I stretched my legs under garish neon lights. Before I knew it, I was watching a free acrobatics show at Circus Circus. It felt like appearing in my own chillier version of Fear and Loathing in Las Vegas, except hold the raw ether and swap in the natural high of budget skiing.

With a Wildfire Burning Nearby, Shenandoah National Park is Cracking Down on Campfires

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

(Photo: Joern Siegroth / Getty Images).

As firefighters continue to battle a nearby blaze, Shenandoah National Park is implementing rigid fire restrictions due to exceptionally dry conditions and heightened wildfire risks going into Thanksgiving week.

According to recent reports, in a Facebook post park officials explained: “These restrictions protect public safety given the elevated risk of wildland fires throughout the park. Shenandoah National Park, Skyline Drive and other facilities and services remain open as scheduled.”.

Industry observers note that under these newly introduced restrictions, visitors to the area will have to rethink their cooking plans since they are temporarily unable to build, attend, or maintain open fires anywhere within the park’s boundaries, including in established pits, grates, and in grills. These regulations also apply to picnic areas, shelters, and huts in the park.

These rules also impact backpackers who rely on portable stoves while recreating in the area. Liquid and wood-fuel camp stoves cannot be used within the park until further notice. At the moment, campers can still use canister stoves like Jet Boils and MSR Pocket Rockets.

Industry observers note that this announcement came just one day after the White Oak Flat Fire erupted on U.S. Forest Service land about 50 miles southwest of Shenandoah National Park. Since Friday, the fire has grown to 1,800 acres, with 49% containment. So far, 131 wildland personnel have responded to the fire including handcrews, wildland engines, bulldozers and two helicopters. Wildland firefighters are using active suppression strategies to contain the fire. No evacuations have been reported, and a cause for the fire has yet to be released.

Recent findings suggest that the NPS identifies two primary wildfire seasons in Shenandoah that run from February to May and October through December. Wildfires are relatively common in Virginia during the month of November although the frequency and impacted acreage vary by season and seasonal driving factors like low humidity and breezy weather.

Shenandoah park officials expect these restrictions to remain in place until the region receives enough precipitation to reduce fire risks.

Our 75-plus testers put the winter 2026-27 season’s skis, boards, boots, and layers through their paces to find the gear that delivers no matter the condition, from carving skis that tempt you off the groomers to a heated glove worth the splurge.

Narrower, more fun, and better at handling whatever the mountain hands you.

Dynastar M-Cross 88 Frontside Ski.

Salomon S/Pro Alpha C BOA Ski Boot.

Not sure what the mountain has in store? Grab the M-Cross 88 and find out. This ski bridges carving and all-mountain categories and is designed for intermediates leveling up, as well as confident skiers looking to play. Its 14-meter turn radius is just a suggestion—we found it equally as game in moguls and tight trees as on wide-open groomers. Dynastar’s Hybrid Core 2.0 (wood plus polyurethane) delivers a damp, poppy feel no matter the terrain. “It’s a wicked fun carving ski that’s up for a little adventure off the beaten path,” one tester said. “It coaxes you into a turn and cradles you there so smoothly I was almost rocked to sleep.”.

According to recent reports, some boots turn heads with upcoming gizmos. The S/Pro Alpha C BOA draws attention with what’s missing: the traditional cuff pivot at the inner ankle. Instead, the cuff flows seamlessly into a low-mounted Powerlink plate—smooth, screw-free, almost Silver Surfer-esque. It’s a radical break from overlap construction, and it delivers two substantial wins: shockingly easy entry for a narrow boot, and an on-snow feel like nothing else in the category. That low Powerlink connection creates a direct line from leg to ski—sensitive and reactive enough that we pushed harder into edge angles, hips dropping closer to the snow than in any other boot we tested. This one’s for skiers who want a snug, locked-in fit and live for the high-performance turn.

According to testers, this is the ski your instructor wants you to have. That’s because the Arcade series’ whole mission is high performance made accessible. The women’s Arcade W 88 pulls it off with a full Titanal layer, a power rail down the wood core, and an hourglass sidecut with a wide, rockered tip. The payoff: excellent edge hold and turn initiation so easy it barely takes pressure to roll onto edge and carve. Its flex spans skill differences too—soft enough for intermediates, strong enough for experts. Groomers are its home turf, but this 88-millimeter-waisted ski held its own in bumps and bashed through crud and chop. It’s a fun, effortless frontside ski that can rip or relax.

Five things every skier and rider should already know—but some need to be reminded.

Two boards and a binding engineered to make sketchy conditions feel like solid ground.

Revamped for 2027 with input from pro rider Nils Mindnich, the Highpath now features a rounded silhouette that floats better in powder and rides switch better, too. Testers loved the ollie power and reliability of its stiff yet lightweight wood core, reinforced with basalt for snap, and fiberglass to dampen a choppy ride. Responsive and powerful without feeling twitchy, it pairs hybrid camber with a raised flat section underfoot, rockered nose and tail, and a quadratic sidecut for toothy edgehold and fluid carves. One tester called it the “most stable board I’ve ridden.” The stiff flex favors experienced riders, and lighter riders may want to size down.

According to recent reports, feeling tentative about the day’s snow or weather report? The Capita Artemis inspires confidence. Camber underfoot, a directional outline, and a medium-stiff wood core reinforced with flax and aramid strips deliver the edgehold and stability to charge through low-vis moguls, launch side hits, and stick solid landings. This deck prioritizes shooting down the fall line at full speed, making it best for advanced riders. Also available in a women’s model.

Sources indicate that bell-to-bell riders and airtime junkies agree: the Union Neo doesn’t make you choose just one riding style. Its lightweight, mid-stiff highback flex brings heel-to-toe stability without the bulk. EVA-padded ankle straps lock in a cozy, hot-spot-free fit. “Good in any aggressive terrain,” one tester noted. “Responsive and strong.” The adjustable baseplate and dual-density bushings soak up everything from overshot park jumps to spring mank, with zero chatter underfoot.

How to blueprint a ski vacation that survives a low-snow winter.

These apparel and accessories don’t need sunshine to look—or perform—their best.

Columbia Roffee Ridge Down Jacket.

Industry observers note that the Moiwa is built for mountain mood swings and kept us riding through frigid mornings and stormy afternoons. A two-layer shell pairs nylon made from recycled fishing nets with a PFAS-free waterproof-breathable membrane, while chest and back fleece panels add warmth. The relaxed freeride fit leaves room for two puffies underneath, while pass pockets, pit vents, a powder skirt, and a helmet-friendly hood round it out. It might be overkill for spring skiing, but for resort days during the coldest months, $400 is a score.

It has been revealed that bold style and serious skiing aren’t mutually exclusive. The Slopestar’s flattering barrel-leg design is built on a three-layer 20K waterproof, windproof membrane that handles everything from spring laps to storm cycles. Thigh vents dump heat, RECCO adds peace of mind, and a restroom-friendly side zip simplifies bathroom breaks. Adjustable suspenders dial in the fit, though shorter torsos may find them too long. Introverts be warned: expect lots of compliments in the lift line.

Industry observers note that small upgrades over several seasons have perfected this pant. A fleece-gripped waistband keeps layers tucked, fleece-lined pockets feel heavenly for parking-lot après, and a thigh pocket opens wide enough for a gloved hand to grab a phone or beacon. PrimaLoft Silver insulation handles temps from negatives into the 40s, while ten-inch thigh vents dump heat fast when things warm up. The two-layer waterproof membrane shrugs off snow and sleet. Between the temp range and details, it’s a tough pant to beat for resort days.

Don’t let the svelte look fool you—this cropped puffer earns its keep on the hill with 650-fill down and Columbia’s Omni-Heat Infinity lining that delivers serious warmth without the bulk. Pit zips let heat escape, and soft thumb loops, generous pockets, and a dedicated ski pass pocket round it out—all at a price that doesn’t punish you for wanting to look good.

Milky, overcast skies play tricks on the eyes—unless you’re wearing the Bollé Cerro. Even with the sky spitting snow and rain, we could see 50 feet ahead, and the cylindrical lens delivered a field of view that rivaled goggles twice its size. Flow Tech venting kept things fog-free on the soggiest days. The lens is fixed, not swappable, but its category 1–3 photochromic tech covers most light conditions, so you don’t have to fuss with a second lens. And at $150, they’re a good value.

Sleek is the name of the game for packs that stay out of your way—on the slopes and on the chairlift. The 18-liter Nirvana is slim enough to ride the lift without shrugging it off, yet roomy enough for extra layers, a thermos or water bottle, snacks, and avalanche safety tools in their own dedicated front pocket. Whether you’re lapping the frontside or strapping on skis to bootpack a ridgeline, the Nirvana has your back.

According to recent reports, expensive? Terribly so. Worth every penny? Absolutely. Heating elements run all the way to the fingertips, powered by 22Wh rechargeable batteries for all-day warmth. Paired with a pre-curved leather shell, brushed liner, and low-bulk PrimaLoft insulation, they’re the warmest, most comfortable heated gloves we’ve tested. Haptic feedback makes adjusting heat levels easy, and a magnetic cuff charger simplifies recharging.

According to recent reports, carv 2 won’t replace a real instructor, but it comes close for a fraction of the cost. Clip the sensors onto your boots and the paired smartphone app breaks down your turns—what you did well, what to fix next—pulling data from 1.5 billion tracked turns and real instructor technique tips. This season, the system gets a notable upgrade: an AI coach you can converse with in plain English. It’s not cheap, but compared to lesson prices, it’s a smart investment if you’re stuck in blue square land and ready to chase black diamonds.

Night skiing is the sport’s best-kept secret.

According to recent reports, night skiing gets filed under “kid stuff,” something you age out of, like ski school and hot cocoa bribes. That’s backward. True, night skiing will never hand you the best run of your life. The snow’s usually chalky or refrozen, the lift is a single slow chair, and the terrain is lit like a parking lot. But none of that matters.

There’s a specific, illicit thrill to skiing after dark that goes back to childhood: staying up past bedtime on a school night, bombing down a green or blue run in a full, devil-may-care pizza, feeling like you’ve gotten away with something—you’re outside after dark in the heart of winter, and that alone makes it great.

It also makes you better. Strip a resort down to one run, and you stop sightseeing and start skiing—really skiing. It’s no coincidence that some of the best alpine skiers in the world were built on hills with just one lift and 300 feet of vertical.

If nothing else, it’s the only time you don’t have to wait in a lift line. Call it kid stuff if you want. Clearly, kids know something the rest of us forgot.

Hike to Over 100 Arches, Hidden Waterfalls, and Towering Cliffs in Kentucky’s Largest Canyon

📅 23 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (839 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Backpacker

💡 Key Takeaways
  • The trail to Natural Bridge will work up a sweat, but the effort is rewarded.
  • While thoroughbred horse racing and barrel-aged bourbon have made Kentucky famous, the state is also home to biodiverse forests and geologically rich mountains.
  • According to recent reports, this ancient canyon spans tens of thousands of acres in eastern/central Kentucky.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The trail to Natural Bridge will work up a sweat, but the effort is rewarded. (Photo: Michelle Polizzi).

While thoroughbred horse racing and barrel-aged bourbon have made Kentucky famous, the state is also home to biodiverse forests and geologically rich mountains. Western Appalachia is a hiker’s paradise, with hundreds of miles of trails, accessing some of the Bluegrass State’s most striking landscapes—and the Red River Gorge is one of its crown jewels.

According to recent reports, this ancient canyon spans tens of thousands of acres in eastern/central Kentucky. The powerful Red River carved the Gorge millions of years ago, creating an outdoor playground of cliffs, creeks, waterfalls, and sculpted rock. It has more than 60 official hiking trails and more sandstone arches than anywhere else in the eastern U.S.

Here’s what to see, where to hike, and how to play if you’ve just got one weekend in Kentucky’s Red River Gorge.

Every first-time visitor to the Red River Gorge must visit Gray’s Arch—no exceptions. This massive natural sandstone structure will give you a crash course in the area’s unique topography, including a diverse hardwood forest, massive rock outcroppings, and steep staircases built directly into the hillsides.

Industry observers note that while most visitors stick to the 2.5-mile out-and-back trail to Gray’s Arch before turning around, it’s worth extending your hike to 5.8 miles on the Gray’s Arch Long Loop Trail. This route takes you past the crowds that gather beneath Gray’s Arch. It winds deeper into the canyon, through the cool, damp forest, over creeks, and beneath looming rock overhangs that still hold Indigenous petroglyphs.

Sources indicate that whittleton Campground has a free day-use lot with a trailhead accessing multiple hikes. Two trails lead to the Whittleton Arch, and another goes to Hensen’s Arch. Try the standard USFS Whittleton Trail, a 2-mile loop that starts and ends at the campground. Or take the longer Whittleton Branch Trail #216. This 4.8-mile out-and-back accesses the arch and follows a creek for most of its length.

According to recent reports, from the campground, you can also hike the Hensen’s Arch Trail. In less than a mile, you’ll reach a second sandstone arch and a deep sinkhole where you can descend into the Earth via a set of metal stairs.

If you’re still feeling adventurous after you hike, head to SUP Kentucky for a Crystal Kayak and SUP Glow Tour, where you’ll paddle underground into a submerged former limestone mine. Thanks to limestone’s natural filtration properties, the water is astoundingly clear. Watch schools of rainbow trout swim beneath your LED-illuminated translucent kayaks, as colors refract upon the ceiling.

The highlight of Kentucky’s Natural Bridge State Resort Park is the massive natural bridge (for which it’s named). This impressive geologic feature stands 65 feet high and 78 feet in length.

Sources indicate that there are several ways to access the arch. Hikers can take the 5.5-mile Natural Bridge and Battleship Rock Trail, which winds past five different trail shelters. Hikers walk beneath some of the country’s tallest tulip poplar trees—some standing more than 150 feet. Natural Bridge is the trail’s climax. You can view the rock formation from numerous vantage points, and even walk across the arch to the lookout point.

Industry observers note that for a longer, more challenging approach, try the 7.5-mile Sand Gap Trail. It can be done as an out-and-back, or connected with Natural Bridge Trail to make a loop.

Recent findings suggest that for more ridge, arch, and canyon trails, head 30 minutes north of the Natural Bridge State Resort Park to the Auxier Ridge Trailhead. From this hub, hikers can access the 6.0-mile Double Arch Loop, which follows Auxier Ridge and passes Courthouse Rock, Haystack Rock, Double Arch, and Arch of Triumph.

The Star Gap and Skyview Arch Trail also starts at the Auxier Ridge trailhead. This roughly 6-mile out-and-back hike is narrow and woodsy. It includes some overgrown sections and short scrambles with about 1,300 feet of elevation gain. But the effort is rewarded with access to Skyview Arch at the end.

Sources indicate that dispersed camping is allowed around Auxier Ridge. Or check out the Sandstone Drifter, a reservable cliffside treehouse accessed by a suspension bridge. But be warned: climbing its 177-stair floating staircase is a short, steep hike in itself.

In a recent development, when rock-climbing traffic slows in winter and early spring, the Muir Valley Nature Preserve is a perfect place to see waterfalls at their full splendor. That’s when precipitation is highest, meaning larger, fuller falls and a chance to see giant icicles and frozen cascades of water. A $15 parking fee is required, and visitors must sign a waiver before entering.

According to recent reports, connect Horseshoe Falls, Joe Ponder Falls, Stadium Wall, and Nellie’s Falls to create a moderate, 4.4-mile hiking loop that spans three waterfalls and winds beneath sandstone overhangs. To extend the hike, add Liz’s Arch and Washboard Wall Trail for an additional 1.5 miles, exposing hikers to more arches, cliffs, and several rock-climbing areas.

Gerber Compleat 16-Piece Cookset.

Some people book a luxury hotel for the weekend. Others would rather throw a tent in the car and figure out where they’re sleeping later. If you have one of the latter on your holiday shopping list, we’ve got you covered. Below are the best camping gifts that will make their time outside a bit more comfortable—even if they swear they don’t care about that. From the practical gear they’ll use on every trip to the fun extras that let them have their creature comforts, these presents will have them plotting their getaway ASAP.

A good pair of hiking socks is always appreciated, but these come with a little extra feel-good factor. Made with 70 percent organic cotton and a cushioned footbed, Conscious Step socks are comfortable enough for long days on the trail (or lazy ones around camp). Even better, purchases support the National Parks Conservation Association, which works to protect America’s public lands.

Sources indicate that this interactive water bottle doubles as an excuse to plan their next significant camping trip. It comes with 63 illustrated, water-resistant stickers representing every national park in the U.S., so they can track where they’ve visited as they go. Since it’s a Nalgene, it’s also durable and featherlight, perfect for hanging from backpacks and gear bags.

This is the ideal gift for the person who considers coffee a nonnegotiable, regardless of how far they’ve wandered from civilization. This compact brewer is roughly the size of a thermos and makes hot coffee and cold brew concentrate in minutes. Simply add finely ground coffee and hot or cold water, let it brew, then use the hand press to dispense a concentrated shot into the included carafe. With no plugs and no charging required, they can throw it in their bag and go.

According to recent reports, camp chairs are great, but they’re not always the easiest things to lug around. This compact stool weighs just 1.2 pounds, folds down to 7.5 inches, and has a swiveling seat that lets you turn without having to pick up and reposition the whole thing. It supports up to 260 pounds, too, which is impressive for its size.

In a recent development, this is a particularly useful piece of gear for any camper who wants to cut down on what they’re carrying. Hydrapak’s collapsible flask has a built-in filter that removes common waterborne bacteria and parasites, allowing hikers to refill from water sources along the trail. It weighs just 4.1 ounces and packs completely flat when empty. It’s a great option for biking, hiking, paddling, and even traveling through sketchy airport bathrooms.

Sources indicate that A headlamp is one of those camping essentials you don’t fully appreciate until you’re stumbling around camp in the dark. The Storm delivers up to 550 lumens with adjustable brightness, three different colored modes (red, blue, and green) to preserve night vision, and a waterproof-rated IPX7 construction that can handle rain and snow. It also has a lock mode to prevent it from accidentally turning on in your pack and draining the batteries before you even reach camp.

If you want your family and friends to experience comfort in camp, look no further than this hammock. The kit has everything someone needs to set up between two trees, including polyester straps and iron carabiners. The Portable Hammock has a weight capacity of 551 pounds and it exhibits both the toughness and user-friendliness that Jeep is known for: It’s made from durable nylon and conveniently packs away into a built-in pouch that doubles as a pocket when the hammock is set up.

Recent findings suggest that there are hundreds of camp slippers on the market, but few are as truly warm or versatile as Glerups. Made from 100 percent natural wool, they’re naturally temperature-regulating and odor-resistant, so feet stay comfortable without getting swampy. The slip-on design makes them easy to kick off tent-side, while the rubber sole handles dirt, mud, and slippery moss with ease.

Finicky sleepers will love this sleeping bag. The Kelty Eclipse skips the traditional zipper in favor of a clever wraparound design that campers spread out when they’re hot or cocoon themself when they’re cold. What it lacks in zippers it makes up for in thoughtful details, including a self-sealing foot vent, oversized hood to keep pillows in place, and internal pockets. It’s also rated to 15 degrees Fahrenheit, so it’s built for more than just balmy summer nights.

A good outdoor blanket earns its keep in just about every situation, and Yeti’s Lowlands is designed to handle more than one night under the stars. Its waterproof, puncture-resistant bottom keeps damp ground from seeping through, while the cushioned top provides a comfortable place to sit, stretch out, or let the dog settle in. Roll it up for transport, then bring it out for everything from picnics to beach days to tailgates.

Sources indicate that if their cooking kit is just a recycled takeout container and one random spork, please get them this Gerber set. The 16-piece set includes a saute pan, stock pot, hot pad, and tableware for four people, giving them everything they need to make and serve a proper meal without cobbling together a kitchen from mismatched gear. When they’re finished, everything nests together for easy packing until the next time they need it.

Sources indicate that these are the pants they’ll put on once at camp and have absolutely no interest in taking off, especially in colder temps. The Fernos pair a cozy insulated interior with a water-resistant exterior, making them ideal for chilly mornings, lounging around the campsite, or layering over a base layer when snow starts to fall. In other words, they’re very durable sweatpants.

According to recent reports, this is about as close as campers can get to bringing their mattress into the woods. The 3.9-inch memory foam pad is thick, supportive, and genuinely comfortable—more proper bed than half-deflated sleeping pad situation. It’s not designed for backpacking (don’t try to carry this on a thru-hike), but it’s portable enough to toss in the car for weekend camping trips. It rolls up tightly for storage and transport and self-inflates when unrolled, making set-up a breeze.

One of the best things about Luno’s car camping mattresses is that they’re not reserved for people with tricked-out 4x4s. The Air Pro is designed to fit a wide range of vehicles, with custom-fit options for dozens of makes and models. This particular kit includes a luxe inflatable mattress, air pump, fitted sheet, pillow, and window screen set that turns their backseat into a dreamy place to sleep. Simply put in their car’s year, make, and model and choose their window size for the gift of spontaneous overnights and long road trips.

Sources indicate that this is for the camp chef who thinks camping dinner should involve way more than hot dogs and s’mores. The Gozney Tread is a portable pizza oven that heats up to 950°F and cooks a delicious pie in about a minute. Its compact design makes it shockingly easy to transport and it runs on propane, so they won’t need to fuss with building a fire. Sure, it’s a bit of a splurge for the campsite, but the lucky recipient will have no trouble convincing their camping buddies it’s worth the extra trunk space.

All campers know that a tent you can properly stand up in is the gift that keeps on giving. The Aurora Highrise has near-vertical walls and a roomy interior that comfortably accommodates up to six people, making it a good pick for families or groups who don’t love sleeping elbow-to-elbow. Large windows and doors let in plenty of light and airflow, while Nightlight Pockets let headlamps and flashlights cast an ambient glow. There’s also a generous vestibule for stashing muddy boots, camping chairs, and anything else that needs protection overnight.

12 Gifts That Backpacker’s Editors Actually Want for the Holidays

Fractel T-SIERPINKSKI Trucker Hat.

Gossamer Gear Thinlight Foam Rolled Pad.

Harvest Right Countertop 360 Freeze Dryer.

Industry observers note that we love outdoor gear, but it’s hard to think of something we need less: Year-round, Backpacker‘s editors test tents, footwear, kitchen gear, and the rest of the latest and greatest hiking equipment to hit the market, and our closets are full to bursting. Still, every once in a while, something comes around that impresses us so much, we’re still thinking about it long after it’s been replaced or passed on to another tester.

In a recent development, we asked our editors to share the gear that’s at the top of their wishlist right now. Some of these wants are modest—a gourmet backpacking meal, a closed-cell foam pad, a trucker hat. Others, like an American-made packraft or a home freeze-dryer, are not. All of it is exceptional. Whether you’re shopping for a hiker who seems like they have everything or adding to your own wish list, this gear is far from ordinary.

It has been revealed that on Backpacker’s recent Editors’ Choice trip along Wisconsin’s Ice Age Trail, we used 10-liter Ursack bear bags to keep our smellables safe, and I fell in love with them. They’re lightweight at just 7.6 ounces, made with bullet-proof Spectra Fabric, and compress as you eat your way through their contents. I wouldn’t throw out my trusty hard canister if I got an Ursack for the holidays, but I’d sure use it a lot. —Will Brendza, Associate Editor.

There are so many flashlights out there, and they range in quality from amazing to shoddy, that I have shied away from actually shopping for one for years. But the LD31 RENEGADE flashlight from Fenix jumped out at me recently. Not only does this puppy pack 3200 lumens in a perfectly sized 5-inch package, but its rechargeable battery also doubles as an emergency external charger and can easily attach to a backpack strap, pocket, or bill of a cap thanks to a two-way clip. On top of all of that, this thing is completely dustproof and waterproof up to 2 meters. —WB.

I tend to be pretty picky when it comes to outdoor and hiking hats. A lot of them look dorky, use cheap materials, or aren’t comfortable when you wear them. That’s why I was so stoked to find Fractel—a running hat tech giant from Australia that blows most American outdoor hats away. The T-SIERPINKSKI Trucker Hats are stylish, lightweight, breathe well, and come in some wild colorways.—WB.

According to recent reports, leave it to Hyperlite to launch a product I didn’t know I needed, can’t really afford, and desperately want right before the holidays. The brand, known for its ultralight packs and shelters, relaunched its apparel line in 2026, and in November dropped an anorak made with waterproof 3-layer Dyneema. It weighs just 7.5 ounces. Do I need a new anorak? Absolutely not. Would I love to keep this sweet little number in my backpacking kit? You bet. —WB.

I’m not usually the kind of hiker who’s willing to give up a hip belt on my pack, but the Volpi FastPack 30 was so much fun to use, it made me want to bring less stuff just so I could justify using it. The vest-style carry on this frameless model was comfortable, and stretch storage pockets on the straps and at the bottom (for a rain shell), plus a strap on top for carrying my sleeping pad, made organization simple. —Adam Roy, Editor-in-Chief.

Sources indicate that if I have a superpower, it’s being able to sleep anywhere, under any circumstances. Why not take advantage of that? I wouldn’t call Gossamer Gear’s Thinlight pads comfortable—at an eighth of an inch thick, they barely qualify as pads at all—but at just 2.7 ounces, they put even most cut-down closed-cell foam pads to shame when it comes to weight. —AR.

There’s a lot to like about the Soto Windmaster, which our testers picked out as the best backpacking stove of 2026. At just 3.1 ounces, it’s featherweight, and it performs consistently in the worst conditions, putting out a reliable flame without chewing through its gas supply even when it gets breezy. Thanks to its regulated design, it’s a solid pick for winter camping, too—a situation where some of my lightweight canister stoves have struggled. —AR.

I’ve used a wide variety of inflatable craft during my time at Backpacker, from paddleboards to canoes. But few have impressed me as much as Alpacka’s Chinook, which tracked steadily and sliced through the water on an early-summer trip through Ruby Horsethief Canyon on the Colorado River. With its prominent bow and stern and removable skeg, the Chinook has some kayak DNA in its design, and paddles more like one than some of the squirrelly packrafts I’ve used. At 9.1 pounds, it’s light enough to haul, and in-tube storage and a clip-in point for a deck bag give it enough capacity for deep backcountry expeditions. —AR.

After more than a decade of use, my trusty lightweight tent from Brooks Range Mountaineering (RIP) is about to give up the ghost. (The organization closed in 2018, if that tells you anything about how long I’ve been using it.) In my search for a replacement, I got to test out an X-Dome this fall, and I now see what all the fuss is about. This tent has a cult following for a reason: It’s featherweight at 44 ounces but doesn’t skimp on livability; the tall ceiling feels like a luxury for sitting up and changing inside. A simple pitch and details like the large doorways and generous internal pockets put this at the top of my list. —Zoe Gates, Senior Editor.

Food is my love language and there’s nothing better than a consumable gift. I evangelize Stowaway Gourmet freeze dried meals to my backpacking friends any chance I get, because they are just so darn tasty. Perfect for a stocking stuffer, or spring for a 72-meal variety pack to feed your favorite hiker for a year. My faves: Drunken Noodles, Kimchi Jigae, Wild Boar Bacon Stew, and Cereal Killer. —ZG.

It has been revealed that the time has come: After years on the trail, I am finally over inflating my sleeping pad manually. Over the years, I’ve tried all the methods, from lung power to foot pumps to inflation sacks. I’m ready to take one dreaded camp chore off my plate. A pad inflator is the height of luxury, and I can’t wait to indulge. —ZG.

If someone really wants to spoil me this year, they’ll invest in a hobby I’ve always wanted to try: freeze drying my own backpacking meals. A dehydrator is an affordable gateway to the world of homemade trail meals, but freeze dryers (larger, more expensive) open up a whole new world of food preservation. Freeze dried meals last longer than dehydrated ones, and maintain better texture and nutritional value—not to mention the wider range of ingredients that hold up to freeze drying. Armed with this appliance, I can spend my whole winter prepping meals for summer backpacking trips—and create some stocking stuffers of my own for the next holiday season. —ZG.
